review.headline: A sharp Exchange French undone by tactical oversights in the center

sections.text: You opted for the Exchange Variation against the French Defense with 3.exd5 exd5. When Black challenged your bishop with 5...h6, you maintained the pin on the f6-knight with 6.Bh4, allowing Black to expand immediately with 6...g5. Capturing with 6.Bxf6 instead would have inflicted structural damage on Black's kingside.

The game heated up after Black traded on f3 and re-routed their knight toward your d4-pawn. You missed the direct danger to your center and played 14.Qe2, which allowed Black to snap off the pawn with 14...Nxd4. Fortunately, Black let you back into the contest by choosing 15...Nxb5 instead of consolidating their extra material.

You quickly anchored your knight on d6, but with Black's knight arriving on h5 to pressure your bishop on g3, tension peaked. Instead of addressing the double attack on your minor pieces with 19.Nf5, you played 19.Rae1. Black eliminated your bishop with 19...Nxg3, and after 20.fxg3, your d6-knight was left completely undefended, dropping to 20...Qxd6.

review.turning_point: The decisive collapse came on 19.Rae1, where ignoring the pressure on g3 and d6 allowed Black to win a full piece after 19...Nxg3 20.fxg3 Qxd6.
review.focus: Keep strict track of overloaded and hanging pieces before committing to central doubling, as 14.Qe2 and 19.Rae1 both left critical material undefended.
